claim: Motor learning occurs through interactions between the cerebellar circuit and cellular plasticity at different sites.
source: Motor learning occurs through interactions between the cerebellar circuit and cellular plasticity at different sites.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: A single complex-spike response driven by one instruction for learning causes short-term plasticity in a Purkinje cell's mossy fiber/parallel-fiber input pathways.
source: 1) a single complex-spike response driven by one instruction for learning causes short-term plasticity in a Purkinje cell's mossy fiber/parallel-fiber input pathways
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing trial-over-trial depression following CS responses.

claim: Complex-spike responses and simple-spike firing rate are correlated across the Purkinje cell population.
source: 2) complex-spike responses and simple-spike firing rate are correlated across the Purkinje cell population
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and demonstrated through population-level analysis.

claim: Simple-spike firing rate at the time of an instruction for learning modulates the probability of a complex-spike response, possibly through a disynaptic feedback pathway to the inferior olive.
source: 3) simple-spike firing rate at the time of an instruction for learning modulates the probability of a complex-spike response, possibly through a disynaptic feedback pathway to the inferior olive.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing correlation between simple-spike firing rate and CS probability.

claim: Long-term potentiation (LTP) has heavily influenced thinking about how the brain learns.
source: Our thinking about how the brain learns has been influenced heavily by the discovery of a form of synaptic plasticity called long-term potentiation (aka 'LTP').
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Behavioral learning involves multiple forms of plasticity at multiple sites in an essential neural circuit for the behavior.
source: Our premise is that behavioral learning involves multiple forms of plasticity at multiple sites in an essential neural circuit for the behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a premise of the study in the introduction.

claim: Different forms of plasticity may be deployed at different sites over different time courses during learning.
source: Different forms of plasticity may be deployed at different sites over different time courses during learning.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: Many forms of cellular plasticity are present in the cerebellum.
source: Many forms of cellular plasticity are present in the cerebellum (Hansel et al., 2001; Zheng and Raman, 2010; Carey, 2011; Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: There is a prominent theory of cerebellar motor learning based on climbing-fiber induced long-term depression of the synapses from parallel fibers to Purkinje cells.
source: The cerebellar circuit is understood well, and there is a prominent theory of cerebellar motor learning (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito, 1972) based on climbing-fiber induced long-term depression of the synapses from parallel fibers to Purkinje cells (Ito and Kano, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational theoretical work.

claim: Research in intact, learning animals using neural recordings, inactivation methods, and genetically-altered mice supports the cerebellar learning theory broadly.
source: Research in intact, learning animals using neural recordings, inactivation methods, and genetically-altered mice supports the cerebellar learning theory broadly (e.g., Gilbert and Thach, 1977; Lisberger, 1994; Medina et al., 2000; Christian and Thompson, 2003; van Alphen and de Zeeuw, 2002; Boyden et al., 2004; Blazquez et al., 2006; Ke et al., 2009; Wulff et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Learning occurs at multiple neural sites and over several time scales.
source: As research on motor learning has advanced, we have come to understand that learning occurs at multiple neural sites and over several time scales (Medina and Mauk, 2000; van Alphen and de Zeeuw, 2002; Jorntell and Ekerot, 2003; Boyden et al., 2004; Yang and Lisberger, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The cerebellar circuit includes a mossy-fiber/granule-cell/parallel-fiber pathway to Purkinje cells, and a climbing fiber pathway that originates in the inferior olive.
source: The cerebellar circuit (Figure 1) includes a mossy-fiber/granule-cell/parallel-fiber pathway to Purkinje cells, and a climbing fiber pathway that originates in the inferior olive (IO).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Parallel-fiber inputs cause conventional action potentials in Purkinje cells known as 'simple-spikes'.
source: The parallel-fiber inputs cause conventional action potentials in Purkinje cells known as 'simple-spikes'.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: An action potential on the climbing-fiber input causes an unconventional, long-duration event known as a 'complex-spike' or 'CS'.
source: An action potential on the climbing-fiber input causes an unconventional, long-duration event known as a 'complex-spike' or 'CS'.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: The cerebellar circuit formulation includes plasticity of Purkinje cell simple-spike responses driven by conjunction of parallel fiber and climbing fiber inputs.
source: Our formulation of the cerebellar circuit includes plasticity of Purkinje cell simple-spike responses driven by conjunction of parallel fiber and climbing fiber inputs (light pink shading in Figure 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The cerebellar circuit includes a disynaptic pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive that includes two inhibitory synapses.
source: a disynaptic pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive that includes two inhibitory synapses (light gray shading in Figure 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Simple-spike firing rate predicts the probability of a complex-spike response to an instruction on a given trial.
source: First, we demonstrate that simple-spike firing rate predicts the probability of a complex-spike response to an instruction on a given trial
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The disynaptic inhibitory pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive causes the correlation between simple-spike firing rate and complex-spike probability.
source: and we suggest that the disynaptic inhibitory pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive causes this correlation (gray shading in Figure 1, De Zeeuw et al., 1998; D'Angelo, 2010; Bengtsson and Hesslow, 2006).
evidence: This is suggested based on anatomical knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Feedback from Purkinje cells might allow the cerebellum to control some of the error signals that guide synaptic plasticity in the cerebellum.
source: Feedback from Purkinje cells might allow the cerebellum to control some of the error signals that guide synaptic plasticity in the cerebellum (Mauk and Donegan, 1997; Kenyon et al., 1998; Miall et al., 1998; Bengtsson and Hesslow, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility and supported by citations.

claim: Complex-spike-linked trial-over-trial depression of simple-spike responses is an expression of short-term plasticity, presumably in the mossy-fiber/parallel-fiber input pathways.
source: Second, we provide evidence that complex-spike-linked trial-over-trial depression of simple-spike responses (Medina and Lisberger, 2008) is an expression of short-term plasticity (pink shading in Figure 1), presumably in the mossy-fiber/parallel-fiber input pathways.
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data and prior work.

claim: A complex-spike response on one learning trial leads to a trial-over-trial depression of simple-spike responses on the subsequent trial.
source: One of our previous papers (Medina and Lisberger, 2008) demonstrated that a complex-spike (CS) response on one learning trial leads to a 'trial-over-trial' depression of simple-spike responses on the subsequent trial.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work.

claim: The depression of simple-spike responses is expressed selectively over a brief interval centered at the time when the instruction occurred.
source: The depression is expressed selectively over a brief interval centered at the time when the instruction occurred.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the trial-over-trial depression.

claim: Pursuit eye movements show trial-over-trial learning when a monkey pursues a target motion with a change in direction.
source: Another of our papers (Yang and Lisberger, 2010) showed that pursuit eye movements show 'trial-over-trial' learning when a monkey pursues a target motion with a change in direction.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work.

claim: The eye velocity on one trial undergoes a transient and properly-timed deflection that takes the eyes in the direction of the change in target motion on the previous trial.
source: The eye velocity on one trial undergoes a transient and properly-timed deflection that takes the eyes in the direction of the change in target motion on the previous trial.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of trial-over-trial learning.

claim: Visual targets start moving in one direction and, 250 ms later, undergo a change in direction in the learning paradigm.
source: In other words, visual targets start moving in one direction and, 250 ms later, undergo a change in direction.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Pursuit learns to anticipate the change in target direction, leading to a small deviation in the direction of eye velocity after a single learning trial.
source: Pursuit learns to anticipate the change in target direction, leading to a small deviation in the direction of eye velocity after a single learning trial, and larger learned changes over blocks of 100 identical learning trials.
evidence: This describes the behavioral learning observed in the study.

claim: Target motion began at a speed of 20 deg/s downward in the pursuit direction.
source: Target motion began at a speed of 20 deg/s downward, in what we will call the 'pursuit' direction.
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters.

claim: 250 ms after the onset of target motion, the target underwent an instructive change in direction through the addition of a rightward or leftward ramp of motion at 30 deg/s for 400 ms.
source: Then, 250 ms after the onset of target motion, the target underwent an 'instructive' change in direction through the addition of a rightward or leftward ramp of motion at 30 deg/s for 400 ms (horizontal position traces in Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters and is illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The random-order learning paradigm allows study of trial-over-trial learning while preventing any long-term learning.
source: This 'random-order' learning paradigm has the advantage that it allows us to study trial-over-trial learning while preventing any long-term learning.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: Trial-over-trial learning causes the eye movement on any given test trial to possess a small, properly-timed deflection that takes eye velocity in the direction of the change in target motion on the prior instruction trial.
source: Trial-over-trial learning causes the eye movement on any given 'test' trial to possess a small, properly-timed deflection that takes eye velocity in the direction of the change in target motion on the prior 'instruction' trial.
evidence: This describes the behavioral outcome of trial-over-trial learning.

claim: Floccular Purkinje cells play important roles in both normal pursuit and pursuit learning.
source: We recorded from Purkinje cells in the floccular complex of the cerebellum because prior research has demonstrated that they play important roles in both normal pursuit (Miles and Fuller, 1975; Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978) and pursuit learning (Kahlon and Lisberger, 2000; Medina and Lisberger, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as rationale for the recording site and supported by citations.

claim: Under normal, pre-learning conditions, the simple-spike firing rate of floccular Purkinje cells is tuned for the direction of pursuit.
source: Under normal, pre-learning conditions, the simple-spike firing rate of floccular Purkinje cells is tuned for the direction of pursuit.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Opposite direction-tuning for simple-spike and CS responses is a general rule in the floccular complex.
source: Opposite direction-tuning for simple-spike and CS responses is a general rule in the floccular complex.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation from the data.

claim: For instructions in the off-direction for simple-spike firing, the CS responses occurred with a high probability in response to the instruction.
source: For instructions in the off-direction for simple-spike firing (Figure 2D), the CS responses occurred with a high probability in response to the instruction.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: For instructions in the on-direction for simple-spike firing, the low spontaneous rate of CS responses was inhibited by the instruction.
source: For instructions in the on-direction for simple-spike firing (Figure 2E), the low spontaneous rate of CS responses was inhibited by the instruction.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Simple-spike firing rate at the time of an instruction was approximately 5 spike/s higher on average depending on whether or not a CS occurred later in the trial in response to an off-direction instruction.
source: Simple-spike firing rate at the time of an instruction was ∼5 spike/s higher on average depending on whether or not a CS occurred later in the trial in response to an off-direction instruction.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative observation from the data.

claim: The relationship between simple-spike and CS responses was restricted to the time interval surrounding the onset of the instruction.
source: The relationship between simple-spike and CS responses was restricted to the time interval surrounding the onset of the instruction (vertical dashed line in Figure 3C,D), suggesting that the relationship is not caused by low frequency fluctuations of attention or other top-down influences.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The increased simple-spike firing rate preceded the time of the CS response and therefore cannot be attributed to bleed-through of the CS spike into the train of spikes used to calculate simple-spike firing rate.
source: Note that the increased simple-spike firing rate preceded the time of the CS response and therefore cannot be attributed to a trivial explanation such as bleed-through of the CS spike into the train of spikes used to calculate simple-spike firing rate.
evidence: This is stated as a control for a potential confound.

claim: On average, the magnitude of simple-spike firing rate averaged 66, 84, and 103 spikes/s for the three segments of the distributions and the probability of a CS response averaged 0.26, 0.34, and 0.44.
source: On average, the magnitude of simple-spike firing rate averaged 66, 84, and 103 spikes/s for the three segments of the distributions and the probability of a CS response averaged 0.26, 0.34, and 0.44.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Correlation analysis of the cluster of points in Figure 3E yielded a statistically-significant correlation of 0.33 (p<<0.001).
source: Correlation analysis of the cluster of points in Figure 3E yielded a statistically-significant correlation of 0.33 (p<<0.001).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: One spike/s of simple-spike firing rate is associated with a difference of 0.005 in the probability of a CS response to the instruction.
source: The slope of the means from the marginal histograms indicated that one spike/s of simple-spike firing rate is associated with a difference of 0.005 in the probability of a CS response to the instruction.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Simple-spike firing rate may modulate the probability of CS responses, but weakly.
source: We conclude that simple-spike firing rate may modulate the probability of CS responses, but weakly.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: For the interval at the end of the pulse of instructive target motion in the on-direction for simple-spike responses, the relationship is quite weak between the probability of a CS and simple-spike firing rate at the time of the instruction.
source: For the interval at the end of the pulse of instructive target motion in the on-direction for simple-spike responses, the relationship is quite weak between the probability of a CS and simple-spike firing rate at the time of the instruction (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The cluster of points in Figure 3F yielded a correlation of −0.028 that was not statistically significant (p=0.65).
source: The cluster of points in Figure 3F yielded a correlation of −0.028 that was not statistically significant (p=0.65)
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: Same-trial facilitation reflects an important feature of cerebellar learning.
source: The existence of same-trial facilitation (Miall et al., 1998) raises the possibility we will consider in our 'Discussion', that same-trial facilitation reflects an important feature of cerebellar learning (Mauk and Donegan, 1997; Kenyon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility to be discussed, supported by citations.

claim: Plasticity of simple-spike firing is linked to the occurrence of a CS response to an instruction.
source: Our second observation shows that plasticity of simple-spike firing is linked to the occurrence of a CS response to an instruction.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Trial-over-trial depression in simple-spike firing rate appeared if the instruction trial contained a CS response to the instruction and the test trial did not.
source: Trial-over-trial depression in simple-spike firing rate appeared if the instruction trial contained a CS response to the instruction and the test trial did not (Figure 4A, red trace, '1-0' pairs)
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Trial-over-trial depression did not appear when neither trial contained a CS response.
source: trial-over-trial depression did not appear when neither trial contained a CS response (Figure 4A, blue trace, '0-0' pairs).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The existence of same-trial facilitation means that trial-over-trial depression could appear simply because of elevated simple-spike firing rate on the instruction trial, but not on the test trial.
source: However, the existence of 'same-trial facilitation' means that trial-over-trial depression could appear simply because of elevated simple-spike firing rate on the instruction trial, but not on the test trial.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the interpretation of the data.

claim: CS-linked short-term plasticity is one component of trial-over-trial depression.
source: Thus, our next step is to take advantage of a dramatically larger dataset than we had before (Medina and Lisberger, 2008) to show that CS-linked short-term plasticity is one component of trial-over-trial depression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis.

claim: Even with the effect of same-trial facilitation nulled, there is a difference in trial-over-trial depression of about 5 spikes/s between '1-1' pairs and '0-0' pairs.
source: Even with the effect of same-trial facilitation nulled, the upper graph of Figure 4A shows a difference in trial-over-trial depression of about 5 spikes/s between '1-1' pairs (green trace) and '0-0' pairs (blue trace).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative observation from Figure 4A.

claim: This component of trial-over-trial-depression is attributed to CS-linked plasticity that occurs during trial-over-trial behavioral learning.
source: We attribute this component of trial-over-trial-depression to CS-linked plasticity that occurs during trial-over-trial behavioral learning, because it persists after we control for same-trial facilitation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Trial-over-trial learning in eye velocity is closely aligned to the trial-over-trial changes in simple-spike firing rate for the 4 pairs of trials.
source: Finally, trial-over-trial learning in eye velocity (Figure 4D) is closely aligned to the trial-over-trial changes in simple-spike firing rate (Figure 4A) for the 4 pairs of trials, supporting a causal link between trial-over-trial depression in neural firing and trial-over-trial learning in behavior.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supporting a causal link.

claim: The CS responses are highly correlated across the Purkinje cell population.
source: As we have noted elsewhere (Medina and Lisberger, 2008), the fact that the learned eye velocities track the trial-over-trial changes in simple-spike firing rate implies that the CS responses are highly correlated across the Purkinje cell population.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claim: Comparison of different pairs revealed statistically significant differences among the four types of pairs of trials for simple-spike firing (p<0.01) and eye velocity (p<0.05).
source: Comparison of different pairs revealed statistically significant differences among the four types of pairs of trials (multiple comparisons in a two-way ANOVA, n = 90 neurons, simple-spike firing, p<0.01; eye velocity, p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: Same-trial facilitation is very weak at the offset of on-direction instructions.
source: Same-trial facilitation is very weak at the offset of on-direction instructions (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Comparison of the trial-over-trial changes in firing rate for '1-0' pairs and '0-0' pairs revealed about 5 spikes/s of CS-linked trial-over-trial depression in simple-spike firing rate at the offset of on-direction instructions.
source: However, comparison of the trial-over-trial changes in firing rate for '1-0' pairs and '0-0' pairs revealed about 5 spikes/s of CS-linked trial-over-trial depression in simple-spike firing rate (bottom graph in Figure 4A, also Medina and Lisberger, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative observation from Figure 4A.

claim: The difference in the firing rate averaged across the simple-spike analysis interval was statistically-significant (paired t-test, p=0.002, n = 90).
source: The difference in the firing rate averaged across the simple-spike analysis interval was statistically-significant (paired t-test, p=0.002, n = 90).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: The presence of trial-over-trial depression in conditions that lack same-trial facilitation implies that trial-over-trial depression is caused partly by plasticity of simple-spike firing that is linked to CS responses.
source: The presence of trial-over-trial depression in conditions that lack same-trial facilitation, albeit with a slightly different time course, implies that trial-over-trial depression is caused partly by plasticity of simple-spike firing that is linked to CS responses.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claim: Simple-spike firing rate was the same in all three trials of '0-0-0' trios.
source: As expected, simple-spike firing rate was the same in all three trials of '0-0-0' trios (Figure 4B), suggesting that our strategy of isolating trios was successful at controlling the effects of past history.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 4B.

claim: For '0-0-1' trios, the simple-spike firing rate was higher in the third trial as expected from the same-trial facilitation.
source: However, for '0-0-1' trios, the simple-spike firing rate was higher in the third trial (Figure 4C, blue trace) as expected from the same-trial facilitation documented in Figure 3, given the presence of CS response to the instruction.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 4C.

claim: Same-trial facilitation of simple-spike firing rate is related to spontaneous fluctuations in simple-spike firing rate.
source: Because the history was the same for each comparison, the most plausible explanation for the intricacies revealed by Figure 4B,C,E,F is that same-trial facilitation of simple-spike firing rate is related to spontaneous fluctuations in simple-spike firing rate.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claim: The same outside influence might drive simple-spike firing rate and the probability of a CS response in parallel.
source: The same outside influence might drive simple-spike firing rate and the probability of a CS response in parallel.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation.

claim: Higher simple-spike firing rates might operate through disynaptic disinhibition to cause a higher probability of inferior olive (and therefore CS) responses to a given sensory event.
source: Or, higher simple-spike firing rates might operate through disynaptic disinhibition (e.g., Figure 1) to cause a higher probability of inferior olive (and therefore CS) responses to a given sensory event.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation.

claim: The model incorporated trial-to-trial variation in simple-spike responses drawn from a distribution with a mean of 100 spikes/s and a standard deviation of 18 spikes/s, in agreement with recordings.
source: Each individual response, meant to reflect the simple-spike firing rate averaged across the analysis interval used for our data, was drawn from a distribution with a mean of 100 spikes/s and a standard deviation of 18 spikes/s, in agreement with our recordings (data not shown).
evidence: This describes a parameter of the computational model based on experimental data.

claim: The trial-to-trial variation in simple-spike firing rate was correlated at a level of approximately 0.16 between pairs of model Purkinje cells.
source: The trial-to-trial variation in simple-spike firing rate was correlated at a level of ∼0.16 between pairs of model Purkinje cells. This level of neuron-neuron correlation enables the neuron-behavior correlations found 250 ms after the onset of pursuit by Medina and Lisberger (2007).
evidence: This describes a parameter of the computational model based on prior findings.

claim: Each inferior olive neuron provided a climbing fiber to 10 Purkinje cells in the model.
source: Each inferior olive neuron provided a climbing fiber to 10 Purkinje cells (Sugihara et al., 2004 visualized at least 5).
evidence: This describes a parameter of the computational model based on anatomical data.

claim: If a model Purkinje cell receives an input from its climbing fiber on a given trial, its simple-spike firing rate on the subsequent trial is reduced by 5 spikes/s through CS-linked plasticity.
source: If a model Purkinje cell receives an input from its climbing fiber on a given trial, its simple-spike firing rate on the subsequent trial is reduced by 5 spikes/s through CS-linked plasticity.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the computational model.

claim: CS-linked plasticity relaxes back to zero over 2 trials when the instruction-test interval is 2.5 s.
source: CS-linked plasticity relaxes back to zero over 2 trials when the instruction-test interval is 2.5 s (Yang and Lisberger, unpublished data).
evidence: This describes a parameter of the computational model based on unpublished data.

claim: The responses of model inferior olive neurons were synchronized enough so that the trial-by-trial correlation in the occurrence of a CS between model Purkinje cells was approximately 0.25 on trials that delivered an off-direction instruction.
source: The responses of model inferior olive neurons were synchronized enough so that the trial-by-trial correlation in the occurrence of a CS between model Purkinje cells was ∼0.25 on trials that delivered an off-direction instruction.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the computational model.

claim: Analysis of the data produced by the model yielded results that captured most of the features of recordings from monkeys.
source: Analysis of the 'data' produced by the model yielded results that captured most of the features of our recordings from monkeys.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the computational modeling.

claim: The model reproduced the finding that each spike/s of simple-spike firing rate is associated with an increase of approximately 0.005 in the probability of a CS response to an off-direction instruction.
source: The model also reproduced our finding that each spike/s of simple-spike firing rate is associated with an increase of ∼0.005 in the probability of a CS response to an off-direction instruction (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the computational modeling.

claim: Almost all of the features of the model were necessary to reproduce the data.
source: Analysis of the sensitivity of the model to its parameters revealed that almost all of the features of the model were necessary to reproduce the data.
evidence: This is stated as a result of sensitivity analysis of the model.

claim: The predictions for trial-over-trial changes in simple-spike firing rate broke down if either CS-linked plasticity or same-trial facilitation was eliminated.
source: The predictions for trial-over-trial changes in simple-spike firing rate broke down if we eliminated either CS-linked plasticity ('NO plast') or same-trial facilitation ('NO SStoCS').
evidence: This is stated as a result of sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Trial-over-trial changes in eye velocity were quite sensitive to the presence of neuron–neuron correlations in the simple-spike firing rate and the CS responses across the population of Purkinje cells.
source: Trial-over-trial changes in eye velocity were quite sensitive to the presence of neuron–neuron correlations in the simple-spike firing rate and the CS responses across the population of Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is stated as a result of sensitivity analysis.

claim: The features included in the model are at least sufficient to reproduce the trial-over-trial changes in simple-spike firing rate and eye velocity in the data.
source: We conclude that the features included in our model are at least sufficient to reproduce the trial-over-trial changes in simple-spike firing rate and eye velocity in our data.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: It is possible that other, quite different, models would make similar predictions.
source: Even though the features of the model are supported by knowledge of the organization of the cerebellar circuit, it is possible that other, quite different, models would make similar predictions.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the modeling results.

claim: The model does not reproduce the absence of same-trial facilitation at the end of an on-direction learning stimulus, when CS-linked plasticity persists.
source: We also note that the model does not reproduce the absence of same-trial facilitation at the end of an on-direction learning stimulus, when CS-linked plasticity persists.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the model.

claim: A learned decrease in simple-spike firing rate may cause a decrease in the probability of CS responses to the instruction through the pathway from Purkinje cells through the deep cerebellar nucleus to the inferior olive.
source: The microcircuit in Figure 1, and its success in modeling our observations on simple-spike firing rate (Figure 5), supports the hypothesis that a learned decrease in simple-spike firing rate may cause a decrease in the probability of CS responses to the instruction, and thereby reduce the magnitude or speed of learning. It could do so through the pathway from Purkinje cells through the deep cerebellar nucleus to the inferior olive.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by the model.

claim: For a random-order learning block, a CS in response to an off-direction instruction on one trial will cause trial-over-trial depression of simple-spike firing rate on the next trial, and if the second trial delivers an off-direction instruction, then the probability of a CS on that trial should be reduced.
source: For a random-order learning block, a CS in response to an off-direction instruction on one trial will cause trial-over-trial depression of simple-spike firing rate on the next trial. If the second trial of a pair delivers an off-direction instruction, then the probability of a CS on that trial should be reduced.
evidence: This is stated as Prediction #1 to be tested.

claim: For the full sample of 90 Purkinje cells, the probability of '1-1' pairs was 0.11 and the probability predicted by independent occurrence of CS responses was 0.12.
source: For the full sample of 90 Purkinje cells, the probability of '1-1' pairs was 0.11 and the probability predicted by independent occurrence of CS responses was 0.12.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result testing Prediction #1.

claim: The difference between the actual and independent probabilities of '1-1' pairs was only 0.01, but it was highly significant (two tailed paired t-test, p<<0.01).
source: Even though the difference between the actual and independent probabilities was only 0.01, it was highly significant (two tailed paired t-test, p<<0.01).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result testing Prediction #1.

claim: The actual probability of '1-0' pairs was 0.24, which was significantly higher than the probability of 0.22 predicted by independence (two tailed paired t-test, p<0.01).
source: The actual probability of 0.24 was significantly higher than the probability of 0.22 predicted by independence (two tailed paired t-test, p<0.01).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result testing Prediction #1.

claim: For a learning block where the same instruction occurs on multiple repeated trials, a gradual learned decrease in simple-spike firing should be associated with a gradual decrease in the probability that a CS occurs in response to an off-direction instruction.
source: For a learning block where the same instruction occurs on multiple repeated trials, a gradual learned decrease in simple-spike firing should be associated with a gradual decrease in the probability that a CS occurs in response to an off-direction instruction.
evidence: This is stated as Prediction #2.

claim: Figure 5B of Medina and Lisberger (2008) verifies Prediction #2.
source: Figure 5B of Medina and Lisberger (2008) verifies this prediction, and our data agree with theirs (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as support for Prediction #2 from prior work.

claim: Past behavioral learning should inhibit future behavioral learning.
source: Past behavioral learning should inhibit future behavioral learning.
evidence: This is stated as Prediction #3.

claim: The longer instruction-test interval of 6 s supports less long-term and trial-over-trial learning than does a shorter instruction-test interval of 2.5 s.
source: The longer instruction-test interval supports less long-term and trial-over-trial learning than does a shorter instruction-test interval (Yang and Lisberger, unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from unpublished data.

claim: The learning in the first 50 trials is lower in amplitude for the 6 s instruction-test interval than for the 2.5 s instruction-test interval.
source: Thus, in Figure 7A,B, the learning in the first 50 trials is lower in amplitude for the 6 s instruction-test interval (open blue symbols) than for the 2.5 s instruction-test interval (open red symbols).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 7A,B.

claim: After switching from a 6 s to a 2.5 s instruction-test interval, the learning curve initiated an increase in learning but the magnitude of learning never caught up to the learning obtained when the short instruction-test interval was used for the entire learning block.
source: After the 50th learning trial, we switched to an instruction-test interval of 2.5 s. The learning curve (Figure 7A,B, filled blue symbols) initiated an increase in learning after the switch from long to short instruction-test intervals, but the magnitude of learning never caught up to the learning obtained when we used the short instruction-test interval for the entire learning block (filled red symbols).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 7A,B.

claim: The effect of past learning was instantiated by as 10 trials of learning, and became slightly stronger as a function of the number of trials that delivered the longer instruction-test interval in the early phase of learning blocks.
source: The effect of past learning was instantiated by as 10 trials of learning, and became slightly stronger as a function of the number of trials that delivered the longer instruction-test interval in the early phase of learning blocks (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 7C,D.

claim: Some past learning inhibits future learning, as predicted if a learned depression of Purkinje cell simple-spike responses inhibits instructive climbing-fiber inputs.
source: We conclude that some past learning inhibits future learning, as predicted if a learned depression of Purkinje cell simple-spike responses inhibits instructive climbing-fiber inputs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the behavioral experiment.

claim: Prior studies have stopped short of monitoring what happens in the cerebellum during behavioral learning.
source: Still, prior studies have stopped short of 'monitoring' what happens in the cerebellum during behavioral learning.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in prior research.

claim: A quantitative description has been created of how CS-linked plasticity of simple-spike firing interacts with the cerebellar circuit in a behaving monkey to create motor learning.
source: We have made the next step of creating a quantitative description of how CS-linked plasticity of simple-spike firing interacts with the cerebellar circuit in a behaving monkey to create motor learning.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: CS-linked trial-over-trial depression of simple-spike firing was demonstrated before.
source: CS-linked trial-over-trial depression of simple-spike firing was demonstrated before (Medina and Lisberger, 2008), and we have verified here that trial-over-trial depression results partly from single-trial plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding that builds on prior work.

claim: CS-related same-trial facilitation of simple-spike firing rate during learning was demonstrated in the present paper.
source: The present paper demonstrates CS-related same-trial facilitation of simple-spike firing rate during learning, and Miall et al. (1998) showed the same phenomenon during quiescence.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Medina and Lisberger (2007) provided evidence for moderate neuron–neuron correlations in simple-spike firing rate within the population of floccular Purkinje cells.
source: Medina and Lisberger (2007) provided evidence for moderate neuron–neuron correlations in simple-spike firing rate within the population of floccular Purkinje cells
evidence: This is stated as support from prior work.

claim: A number of papers have outlined the case for synchrony across the climbing-fiber inputs.
source: and a number of papers have outlined the case for synchrony across the climbing-fiber inputs (Llinas et al., 1974; Welsh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as support from prior work.

claim: The measurements have created a hypothesis for the operation of the cerebellar microcircuit during behavioral learning that is validated by experimental data and computer simulations.
source: Thus, our measurements have created a hypothesis for the operation of the cerebellar microcircuit during behavioral learning that is validated by experimental data and computer simulations.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: Other models also could reproduce the data.
source: Still, we are aware that other models also could reproduce our data.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the conclusions.

claim: The probability of a CS and the simple-spike firing rate at the time of the instruction could be subject to top-down influences in parallel.
source: For example, the probability of a CS and the simple-spike firing rate at the time of the instruction could be subject to top-down influences in parallel, a situation that would not require a pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive, and might alter the implications for what happens in the cerebellum during motor learning.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative explanation.

claim: CS-linked plasticity is responsible for only half of trial-over-trial depression.
source: Indeed, our analysis indicates that CS-linked plasticity is responsible for only half of trial-over-trial depression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis.

claim: The other half of trial-over-trial depression on '1-0' pairs of trials is related to the tendency for simple-spike firing rate to be higher on trials with a CS.
source: The other half of trial-over-trial depression on '1-0' pairs of trials is related to the tendency for simple-spike firing rate to be higher on trials with a CS.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis.

claim: If simple-spike firing rate acts through inhibitory neurons in the deep cerebellar nucleus to modulate the response of inferior olive neurons to a given instruction, then a learned response in the cerebellum could modulate its own instructive inputs.
source: If simple-spike firing rate acts through inhibitory neurons in the deep cerebellar nucleus to modulate the response of inferior olive neurons to a given instruction, then a learned response in the cerebellum could modulate its own instructive inputs (Schweighofer, et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a possible implication supported by a citation.

claim: There are two inhibitory synapses in the pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive.
source: There are two inhibitory synapses in the pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive (De Zeeuw et al., 1998; D'Angelo, 2010)
evidence: This is stated as anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Higher (lower) simple-spike firing could cause a higher (lower) probability of CS responses, in agreement with the data of Miall et al. (1998) during quiescence and with data during learning.
source: so higher (lower) simple-spike firing could cause a higher (lower) probability of CS responses, in agreement with the data of Miall et al. (1998) during quiescence and with our data during learning.
evidence: This is stated as an inference supported by data and citations.

claim: The climbing fiber axons from the inferior olive to the cerebellum and the pathway from the deep cerebellar nucleus back to the inferior olive both cross the midline, so that Purkinje cells can control their own climbing-fiber inputs.
source: Importantly, the climbing fiber axons from the inferior olive to the cerebellum and the pathway from the deep cerebellar nucleus back to the inferior olive both cross the midline, so that Purkinje cells can control their own climbing-fiber inputs (Ruigrok, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as anatomical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: There is a correlation between CS probability and simple-spike firing rate on learning trials.
source: (1) There is a correlation between CS probability and simple-spike firing rate on learning trials.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the data supporting the idea that Purkinje cells modulate their own climbing fiber inputs.

claim: Learned decreases in simple-spike firing are associated with a reduction in the probability of CS responses to an instruction, both during learning blocks that repeat the same instruction on many trials and during single-trial learning.
source: (2) Learned decreases in simple-spike firing are associated with a reduction in the probability of CS responses to an instruction, both during learning blocks that repeat the same instruction on many trials (Medina and Lisberger, 2008) and during single-trial learning.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the data supporting the idea that Purkinje cells modulate their own climbing fiber inputs.

claim: Past learning inhibits future learning, presumably by causing a learned decrease in the simple-spike responses of Purkinje cells that could reduce the probability of the CS responses that would instruct learning.
source: (3) Past learning inhibits future learning, presumably by causing a learned decrease in the simple-spike responses of Purkinje cells (Medina and Lisberger, 2008) that could reduce the probability of the CS responses that would instruct learning.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the data supporting the idea that Purkinje cells modulate their own climbing fiber inputs.

claim: Anatomical and physiological studies have documented the required neural pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive.
source: In addition, anatomical and physiological studies have documented the required neural pathway (Ruigrok, 1997; Bengtsson and Hesslow, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as support from prior work.

claim: The cerebellar learning circuit is set up to be conservative by allowing only a finite amount of learning in the cerebellar cortex.
source: We suggest that the cerebellar learning circuit is set up to be conservative by allowing only a finite amount of learning in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the findings.

claim: Learning may need to be transferred to the deep cerebellar nucleus so that plasticity can relax back to baseline in the cerebellar cortex before further plasticity is allowed in the input pathways to Purkinje cells.
source: Learning may need to be transferred to the deep cerebellar nucleus (Ohyama et al., 2006) so that plasticity can relax back to baseline in the cerebellar cortex before further plasticity is allowed in the input pathways to Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion supported by a citation.

claim: There are multiple possible explanations for the observation that past learning inhibits future learning in pursuit eye movements.
source: Still, we are aware that there are multiple possible explanations for the observation that past learning inhibits future learning in pursuit eye movements.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the interpretation.

claim: The data add support for, but do not obligate the conclusion that Purkinje cells modulate their own climbing-fiber inputs.
source: Thus, our data add support for, but do not obligate the conclusion that Purkinje cells modulate their own climbing-fiber inputs.
evidence: This is stated as a cautious conclusion from the data.

claim: CS-linked plasticity of simple-spike responses in the data is expected to be a product of CS-driven depression of the synapses from parallel fibers to Purkinje cells.
source: We expect that the CS-linked plasticity of simple-spike responses in our data is a product of CS-driven depression of the synapses from parallel fibers to Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation about the mechanism.

claim: Cannabinoid-dependent synaptic depression seems to have the requisite brief time course for CS-linked plasticity.
source: For example, cannabinoid-dependent synaptic depression seems to have the requisite brief time course (Brown et al., 2003; Brenowitz and Regehr, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a possible mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Other forms of cellular plasticity may contribute, either within the cerebellar cortex or in the deep cerebellar nucleus.
source: However, other forms of cellular plasticity may contribute, either within the cerebellar cortex (Hansel et al., 2001; Carey, 2011) or in the deep cerebellar nucleus (Miles and Lisberger, 1981; Zhang and Linden, 2006; Zheng and Raman, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility supported by citations.

claim: The oculomotor vermis also could play a role in pursuit learning.
source: The oculomotor vermis also could play a role in pursuit learning (Suzuki and Keller, 1988; Takagi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility supported by citations.

claim: Future work will provide positive evidence of specific roles during learning for other forms of plasticity and other brain sites of learning.
source: We expect that future work will provide positive evidence of specific roles during learning for other forms of plasticity and other brain sites of learning.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation for future research.

claim: Experiments were conducted on four awake, behaving adult male rhesus monkeys.
source: We conducted experiments on four awake, behaving adult male rhesus monkeys.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Two monkeys were used for recordings from Purkinje cells in the floccular complex during pursuit learning at UCSF.
source: Two monkeys were used for recordings from Purkinje cells in the floccular complex during pursuit learning (at UCSF)
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and procedures.

claim: Two monkeys were used only for behavioral studies of pursuit learning at Duke.
source: and the other two were used only for behavioral studies of pursuit learning (at Duke).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and procedures.

claim: The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at UCSF and Duke had approved all the procedures in advance.
source: The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at UCSF and Duke had approved all the procedures in advance.
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the experiments.

claim: The procedures were in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
source: The procedures were in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
evidence: This describes ethical compliance for the experiments.

claim: Each single neuron recording experiment consisted of two separate blocks: a baseline block comprising approximately 80 trials and a learning block comprising about 400 trials.
source: Each single neuron recording experiment consisted of two separate blocks. The baseline block comprised approximately 80 trials. ... A learning block comprised about 400 trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The analysis is based on 90 out of 108 Purkinje cells that showed CS probabilities more than three times their spontaneous level of 0.09 ± 0.02.
source: Our analysis is based on the large majority of the Purkinje cells (group 1, 90/108) that showed CS probabilities more than three times their spontaneous level of 0.09 ± 0.02 (mean ± SD).
evidence: This describes the data selection criteria.

claim: A subpopulation of 18 out of 108 Purkinje cells whose CS probabilities after an instruction were less than 0.2 and never exceeded three times their spontaneous level was excluded from analysis.
source: We excluded from analysis a much smaller subpopulation (group 2, 18/108), whose CS probabilities after an instruction were less than 0.2 and never exceeded three times their spontaneous level.
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.
